talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Offers a mindset framework for handling stress, information overload and uncertainty through awareness and reframing thoughts.
talks.summary:
In this RVAsec 2022 keynote, Dorsey Levens, a retired NFL running back who later moved into acting and mindfulness teaching, opens by asking the room about the stress people carry. He argues that after the pandemic many people are running on a way of thinking that no longer helps them, and that how we interpret events shapes our feelings more than the events themselves.

The middle of the talk lays out his program, Re.Mind. Listeners are encouraged to notice what they are thinking, to separate what they can control from what they cannot, and to focus on the things they care about most. He covers giving up unsolicited advice, treating setbacks as lessons, and reframing hard moments with a parable about a horse that keeps turning out to be good or bad news depending on what comes later. He compares changing habits to physical training, where repetition over weeks matters more than one strong effort, and points out that most feared outcomes never happen. Examples come from his football career, including a switch from running back to wide receiver that he later saw as useful, and from everyday frustrations such as traffic.

He closes with practical steps: check your inner dialogue, replace fearful or hostile thoughts with more useful ones, reset each morning instead of waiting for a fresh start, and look back at the past only to learn from it. A short Q&A covers staying motivated on low-energy days and how he handled leaving professional sport. The talk contains no technical security content. Its value for practitioners is in its guidance on staying composed under pressure, which applies to incident response and other high-stress work.

talks.title: Honeypot Boo Boo: Understanding Adversaries
talks.teaser: Shows how deception technology such as honeypots can help defenders observe and understand adversary behavior.

talks.title: Slippery SOP: Edge Cases in the Same Origin Policy
talks.teaser: Explores where the browser Same-Origin Policy breaks down, covering cookie scoping, SameSite, and DNS rebinding edge cases.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why cross-site request forgery and cross-site scripting persist when browsers enforce the Same-Origin Policy, and maps the policy's edge cases without covering CORS. An origin is treated as scheme, host and port, and the policy allows embedding of images, scripts and stylesheets while blocking cross-site reads. Fetch and XHR requests are restricted to a few methods and content types, so strict JSON validation adds a useful layer against forged requests. Setting document.domain, by contrast, loosens the boundary across subdomains.

The middle section compares this with cookie scoping. Domain, path, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite each isolate cookies differently, and cookies have no port-based isolation. A subdomain takeover can capture a parent-scoped session cookie or send forged requests that SameSite does not block, since the browser treats sibling subdomains as same-site. Early SameSite bypasses, browser quirks and Edge's exposure of applied CSS rules are noted as well.

The final part covers DNS rebinding, where a hostname moves from a public address to localhost mid-session. Firefox allowed the resulting read, while Chrome's Private Network Access blocked it, and certificate validation stops the attack in secure contexts. Burp Suite's former lack of TLS validation exposed internal HTTPS sites, a gap the vendor has begun to address in an early-adopter build. Practitioners should treat SameSite, tokens and content-type checks as layered defenses rather than complete fixes.

talks.title: Bootstrapping Your First AppSec Program
talks.teaser: Walks through building an application security program from scratch, covering hiring, threat modeling, and winning engineering buy-in.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames application security as a team and a program rather than a stack of scanning tools, aimed at people starting an AppSec function with little or no budget. He argues that the scope includes the code a company writes, third-party libraries and open source dependencies, and that success depends heavily on relationships and leadership. Early hires should combine good communication skills with a working grasp of security, and a small team can grow by learning from the strongest breakers and developers already in the company.

The middle of the talk covers sequencing. He recommends threat modeling before running tools, since it surfaces real exposures such as risky container configuration, and advises rolling out one control at a time with a plan for the whole year. He describes earning buy-in from engineering leaders, starting controls as education rather than blocking gates, and backing them with written policy. He also shares an example where a trimmed, validated list of dynamic scanning findings earned team trust quickly. Embedded security engineers, security champions and lunch-and-learn training are presented as ways to spread knowledge.

He closes with continuous improvement: tuning tools, building metrics that tell a clear story to leadership, and treating engineers as customers. The main takeaway is to start small, earn trust through relationships, and measure progress.

talks.title: Talk the Talk: Communicating Business Risk During Cyber Incidents
talks.teaser: Shows how responders can explain cyber incidents and business risk to executives and win resources afterward.
talks.summary:
The talk focuses on the gap between an incident response team and the business leaders who need information while an incident is still unfolding. Alex Nette explains that executives, customers, regulators, peers and co-workers tend to want the same thing: a clear picture of what happened and a path to restoring operations while protecting the company's reputation. Answering with a vague status line quickly erodes trust.

The middle section offers practical tactics. Map each affected system to the business process it supports, give a time-to-recovery range rather than a non-answer, and ask for specific help such as money, staff, or a short outage leadership can approve. Keep updates flowing as estimates change, and maintain contact lists that account for remote or absent staff. Nette also notes that news coverage tends to highlight dramatic attacks while routine ones like social engineering go underreported, which can skew leadership's view of risk.

The closing portion covers preparation and follow-up. Contingency planning should include things like spare laptops and alternate work sites, and disaster recovery should be tested by actually failing over rather than only discussed in a tabletop exercise. After an event, document a lessons-learned report that ties the incident to business impact. Finally, frame security investments in quantitative terms, estimating loss magnitude and frequency so finance leaders can weigh control costs against expected losses.

talks.title: Warning: This Message Originated from Outside of Your Organization
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers send phishing emails that pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC through trusted SaaS platforms.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that users have become desensitized to external-sender warning banners, and that well-known SaaS platforms can be abused to deliver phishing email. It walks through the usual phishing setup: buying an aged domain, getting it categorized by web filters, publishing SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, and warming the domain up so it does not look suspicious. The speaker notes that such domains often burn quickly, which forces attackers to repeat the work.

The middle of the talk shows two examples. In the first, a free project-management trial sends invitation emails with attacker-controlled body text that pass authentication checks, although some invites were filtered to spam. In the second, an API management invitation template in Azure sends mail from a Microsoft-signed sender with customised display details. A serverless function proxy is then shown acting as a redirector, so traffic appears to end at a Microsoft-owned IP address with a valid certificate. Safe-link scanners can be sidestepped by serving them benign content.

The closing discussion covers defences: requiring domain-ownership verification before SaaS senders can use a company's domain, pointing users to internal portals instead of external links, preparing staff for expected vendor emails, blocking services the organization does not use, and adding content analysis and defence-in-depth layers. The main takeaway is that passing email authentication does not establish trust, and organizations should update their risk models for mail sent through trusted services.

talks.title: Working With The FBI
talks.teaser: Explains how FBI cyber agents engage with victims of intrusions, fraud and ransomware, and what organizations should prepare.
talks.summary:
Two FBI cyber agents from the Richmond field office explain what the Bureau does and how it engages with organizations that have been hit by an intrusion. They outline how the cyber division's strategy flows down from the national mission, how federal policy gives the FBI the lead investigative role alongside DHS and the Defense Department, and how task forces with state and local partners stretch a small agent workforce. A Cyber Action Team, a surge unit of specialists, is described as deploying to large incidents.

Business email compromise receives the most attention as a financial threat. The speakers note that most cases rely on social engineering rather than intrusion, and they urge accounts payable staff to verify payment changes through a pre-established phone number and to add approval layers. Quick reporting matters because an asset recovery team can often freeze transferred funds within a day or two. Ransomware is also covered, including a pipeline case in which seized wallet keys and infrastructure takedowns involved multiple agencies and foreign partners. Investigators target criminal ecosystems and use indictments to limit suspects' travel.

For practitioners, the advice centers on preparation. Build a relationship with the local field office before an incident, maintain a response plan that covers losing key systems, and keep network diagrams current so scope can be understood quickly. Most engagement happens by consent, so legal teams should decide in advance what evidence can be shared, and acceptable-use banners should make monitoring expectations clear. The agents stressed that the FBI does not recommend specific products, remediate networks, or publicize victims.

talks.title: Digital Forensics: Reconstructing an Attack in Modern Web Apps
talks.teaser: Walks through reconstructing a compromised Windows web server, from disk artifacts and registry data to IIS logs and a web shell.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that modern web applications rarely live on one system. They span CI/CD pipelines, container images, cloud services and SaaS tools, so the point where an intrusion began is often far from where its effects show up. The speaker frames digital forensics as evidence collection that must survive scrutiny, with a documented chain of custody, and separates it from incident response. Responders who reboot machines or wipe systems can destroy volatile evidence, so examiners need to work with them early.

The core of the session is a live demonstration on a Windows Server host where an unexpected local administrator account and an unknown running executable had been found. The analysis builds a timeline from user activity artifacts, recycle bin metadata and event logs, then checks the SAM registry hive to confirm which accounts belong to the local administrators group. A service configured with an unquoted executable path is identified as a likely hijack point, since Windows would run a planted program.exe from the C drive. IIS logs then show directory brute-forcing, a Python-driven POST request, and an ASPX web shell reached through an arbitrary file upload flaw in a vulnerable archiving product.

The practical takeaways are to image whole disks including unallocated space, check shadow copies and backups for earlier evidence, and look beyond the initial host to proxies, firewalls and databases. The speaker also stresses that a forensic report outlives the examiner and must be accurate, because it may reach boards or law enforcement.

talks.title: Basslines and Baselines: The role of Anomaly Detection in Cloud Security
talks.teaser: Introduces anomaly detection as a baseline-driven layer for securing cloud-native environments beyond signature rules.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the operational problem of cloud-native security. Microservices, Kubernetes, autoscaling and short-lived addresses make systems harder to understand, while large signature rule sets produce many false positives, break workloads and wear down analysts. Anomaly detection is presented as an additional layer alongside signature tools and hardening, not a replacement for them.

The speaker traces the approach to Dorothy Denning's late-1980s intrusion detection model, which assumed that exploitation shows up as abnormal use of a system. He walks through its components: subjects such as human accounts, service accounts and API keys; objects such as instances, load balancers, clusters and containers; audit records drawn from cloud and Kubernetes logs; and profiles that describe who talks to whom over time. A household analogy illustrates why baselines should be built per environment. The talk also covers the model's limits: attacks that resemble normal traffic, benign changes from fast development, data silos, scaling demands, and attackers who might learn the baseline or flood it with noise. Grouping identical resources is discussed as a way to reduce alert storms.

The closing section points to progress in unsupervised machine learning and scalable architectures that make baselines more practical. Practitioners are advised to test vendors for scale in their own environment, to look for ways to combine signature and anomaly signals, and to correlate weak events rather than judging each one alone.

talks.title: Threat Intelligence 2022 Actionable?
talks.teaser: Walks through the kinds of threat intelligence data in use today and judges whether each one is actionable for a small organization.
talks.summary:
Peter Partyka opens with a short history of threat intelligence, contrasting the feeds of about 2012, built mostly on IP addresses, domains and YARA rules, with what vendors offer now. He introduces a risk equation and a simplified intelligence cycle, then sets up a fictional 200-person company that issues credit cards and later adds SIM cards to its business.

The middle of the session is an audience exercise. Slides show different kinds of intelligence, and the room decides whether each one would be useful to that company. Simple indicators such as a YARA rule or a single IP address can go straight into security devices, but they gain value only when they carry context. Other items, including breach-derived card data, underground chatter about SIM swapping, a finished report on trending vulnerabilities, and lists of commonly used passwords, are not machine-consumable. They still drive decisions for fraud, identity and vulnerability teams.

The closing argument is that usefulness depends on who receives the information and whether they can act on it, not on the data type alone. Partyka argues that raw data becomes intelligence only after collection, processing and analysis, and that the category of intelligence itself needs rethinking for the digital world. He ends by encouraging organizations to share indicators with peers, since shared intelligence is one of the most effective defenses available.

talks.title: To Err is Human: Combating Human Error in Healthcare Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Examines how human error drives costly healthcare data breaches and argues for security that plans around everyday user behavior.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that human error is the top driver of data breaches and that healthcare breaches carry the highest average cost of any industry. It presents breach statistics showing rising costs, per-record expenses for patient data, and how remote work has widened exposure. Audience polls are used throughout to gauge who has seen an organization breached.

To make this concrete, the speaker walks through a composite healthcare organization whose vendor's email account was compromised. Attackers used it to send phishing messages for months, reaching patient and employee records and spreading into other organizations. The cost breakdown covers investigation, notification, lost business and post-breach response. Error types range from misdirected emails and misconfigured cloud services to phishing, and emailed attachments act as an unmanaged file store. Shadow IT appears when security controls get in the way of daily work.

The main takeaway is that policies and tighter controls tend to create exceptions and workarounds, so the cycle repeats. The speaker recommends reducing the number of security decisions users must make, studying actual workflows to fix productivity gaps, offering safe options for remote work, and automating where possible. Existing tools such as multi-factor authentication and password managers are underused, and education should extend beyond phishing drills. Protection should assume that users will sometimes make mistakes.

talks.title: Malware: Where Does It Come From?
talks.teaser: Examines where real-world malware downloads originate, from search results and cloud apps to chat platforms and CDNs.
talks.summary:
The talk asks a simple question: where does malware come from? The speaker draws on roughly 1.2 million malware blocks recorded over about five months, collected by a secure web gateway that covers around 3.1 million users, mostly on managed Windows laptops. Because the data only covers HTTP and HTTPS downloads, phones and other traffic are underrepresented, and the focus is on downloads that were actually blocked rather than everything attackers publish.

The findings challenge the assumption that email is the main route. Most blocked files were ordinary Windows executables and DLLs, and no single malware family dominated. Search engine referrals led people to malicious PDFs built from copied user manual text, titled with very specific product names, and linked to captcha pages and redirect chains. Cloud storage, code hosting and file transfer sites hosted a large share of downloads, and chat platforms were used to lure victims. Content delivery networks and compromised WordPress sites added to the spread, and one infostealer was promoted through a fake cryptocurrency video channel.

The practical takeaway is that category and domain blocking alone will miss much of this traffic. The speaker urges teams to confirm that all web traffic actually passes through their controls, to watch consent grants for third-party apps in cloud suites, and to start from the malware alerts they actually receive and work upstream from there.
